title: When Mountains are Mountains
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer shares that true understanding in Zen practice comes from letting go of our tendency to grasp for fixed truths or judgments, and instead embracing the present moment without attachment or expectation. This means recognizing that truth is not something we can control or understand, but rather it emerges when we stop trying to grasp it. By doing so, we can awaken to the reality of life itself, which is inherently complex, beautiful, and imperfect.

sentences.text: Well, I'm always thinking, what am I going to say to these nice people tomorrow?
So I'm thinking about it during the day.
I know that many of you have been sitting with me for decades, and I'm sure you have already heard everything I could possibly say by now.
What am I going to say that will impress you after all this?
Even though I generally don't repeat any talks, at least not in the same place, I'm sure I just keep saying the same things over and over and over again.
In fact, I'm sure I've said just that, even though I'm trying to have something new to say.

I'm really racking my brains to keep you entertained, but no matter how hard I try, at some point it occurs to me that I keep saying the same things over and over again, or the same one thing, which I guess would happen to any of us if we kept on talking long enough.
But it occurs to me that this is exactly what's happening to all of us.
We are all talking every single day, and we're all saying the same things over and over and over again.

You get the magazine and it has the new article in it that everybody's emailing everybody else about, and it's this brand new idea, which when you think about it is the same idea from before, only wearing a different outfit.
And all the new people are saying the same things that the old people used to say.
It's really amazing, and yet we remain perplexed and we keep thinking, my god, I've never heard that before.
Sometimes you find yourself in a room full of people, maybe at a restaurant, with everybody talking at the same time.
Just listen to the talk, and it's a weird murmuring sound without any words in it.
No meaning, no words.
Kind of like traffic or ocean waves, the music of human voices that rises and falls in pitch.
Maybe the meaning in the end is just musical.
So I've been singing, and we've been singing together this week, the old human songs that we keep on singing over and over again.
And Buddha was also singing songs.
That's what I meant yesterday when I said that Buddha wasn't really concerned about what's right or what's true.
He saw that already there was a problem with the truth.
There's already a problem with the effort to get it right.
So he just wanted to figure out a way to help us so that we wouldn't have to suffer as much.
He kept trying out different songs, different keys, different notes, different rhythms and harmonies, in the hope that just the sound of his voice would somehow offer us some support.
Sometimes he said it this way, sometimes he said it that way.
The texts are full of contradictions.
As I said, mostly Buddha was trying to undo something that we believe rather than give us something to believe.
So really, Buddhism is more about what is not the case than about what is the case.
That's why you may have noticed yesterday, in something I quoted, that the Buddha seemed to be concerned about nihilism and eternalism.
In many places he's concerned about them, which to us is like, what?
Why would you be worried about that?
But the Buddha was really focused on this.
Nihilism to him meant negation.

Since he was always negating the usual concepts and beliefs that he knew were binding us, he realized that he would be subject to being accused of nihilism, of believing in nothing, of holding to no truth.
But he didn't want to do the opposite.

He didn't want to assert something positive, which he called eternalism, because if he asserted something positive, then we would have something to grasp, an implement with which to hit ourselves over the head and other people also.
And this grasping is the basic problem, so he didn't want to encourage it.
He wanted to try to avoid both nihilism and eternalism.
But how can you do this?
Can you even do this?
And what if you could do it?
Then what would you be left with?
And what could you say?
So now I'll tell you another Zen story.
This is a very important and famous story, because it's about the process of our practicing over time.
Since all of us are practicing over time, we want to know what happens over time as we practice.
So here's the story.

*Chan Master Ching Yuan ascended the high seat, the Dharma lecture seat, and he said: "Thirty years ago, before this old monk had begun to practice Chan, I saw mountains as mountains and rivers as rivers.
Then later on, I gained some personal insight and found a way in.
And then I saw that mountains are not mountains and rivers are not rivers.
But now, having reached a place of rest, I once again see that mountains are just mountains and rivers are just rivers.
To all of you, I ask: as for these three ways of understanding, are they the same or are they different?"*
*"Should there be a monastic or a lay person among you who can find a way out of this, you will have met this old monk face to face."*
Usually the story is reduced to the three phases: mountains are mountains, mountains are not mountains, mountains are mountains.
The usual way of understanding the story goes something like this.
When you first start to practice, naturally you see things in a conventional way, the way you were brought up and the way your society sees things, the ordinary way.
You think that there are trees and people, and that there's you and me, and that we all have our needs and desires and so on.
If you come to practice, you come based on that conventional understanding.
You have some reason based on that to come.
You think, well, this would be an interesting experience.
Or you think, I want to have spiritual practice, and this will be one way.
Or maybe you think I'd like to join a community, or maybe you think I have a lot of problems and maybe this will help.
So this is mountains are mountains, rivers are rivers.
But then you take up the practice and you practice for a little while, and little by little you realize you're becoming slightly deranged.
You hear somebody prattling on about emptiness, which sounds strange at first, but you hear it enough and it begins to mean something to you.
You hear somebody going on about how there is no self, or it's not what you thought it was, and at first it sounds weird, but little by little you sort of get it.
You come to sesshin, which is a very unusual thing to do, and you find that it is a powerful and moving experience that challenges your usual way of seeing and living.
Now you're really getting disoriented, and you realize that you're not going to be able to go back to the way things were before.
Then you go home from sesshin and everything looks and feels different and slightly disturbing.
You look at people on the street and you realize that everybody looks desperate.
Before, you just thought it was a bunch of ordinary people, but now you realize that it's a bunch of desperate characters running around in the world.
This is kind of scary.
Everybody looks like they're haunted somehow.
Even your family members seem weird to you, and you really don't know how you're going to explain to them that they too are empty, that no matter what they think, they don't have any selves.
So this whole thing is extremely troubling.
And this means you have now found some personal insight and you have a way in, just as Ching Yuen says, and now your experience is mountains are not mountains, rivers are not rivers.
But then time goes by and you keep on practicing.
You're listening to lots of talks.
Maybe you're reading Dharma books.
You're talking to your Dharma friends.
You're going to the community and practicing with your community.
You're going to more sesshin.
Now you realize that you are paying attention to your life more and more on a moment by moment basis, and you're feeling your life differently.
Little by little, practice just becomes more normal.
It's just your way of life.
Now you come home from sesshin and it's no problem anymore.
Your friends and co-workers and family members no longer seem strange to you, and you just resume your ordinary everyday way of being and seeing things.
Except now maybe there's more depth, a little more calmness, more wisdom, which you can sort of feel, but only if you think about it.
Mostly you don't feel it.
It's just the way it is.
And you forgot the reason that you came to practice.
Whatever it was you thought you were coming for, it's gone.
Now you just practice because, well, that's what you do.
That's who you are.
You have reached a place of some rest.
Mountains are mountains and rivers are rivers.
That's usually the way we appreciate that story.
The theory behind it is called the theory of two truths.
The two truths are the conventional truth and the ultimate truth, and they're both true.
The conventional truth, of course, is the agreed upon screwed up world with all its faulty assumptions that lead to suffering.
The ultimate truth is no self and emptiness, things being not at all as they seem, but deeply otherwise.
With ongoing practice we study and deepen our appreciation of these two truths, and eventually we integrate them.
So we just live an ordinary life.
Maybe we can be happy and do something good for somebody.
That would be nice.
So that's the idea.
When you study the two truths, it's always pointed out to you that there are not two truths.
Emptiness and non-self are not some truth or some reality.
They're just the conventional truth correctly understood, because if there were some other truth, that would be eternalism.
So the real truth isn't anything.
It's just ordinary things.
That's why you end up with mountains are mountains.
No special something.
Just life.
So this all makes a lot of sense, right?
That's the problem.
It makes too much sense.
It's no good.
As soon as you're making sense, you right away say, oh, I'm falling into the trap of eternalism.
I have a viewpoint that I think is right.
I have something to grasp.
And my little graspy habit is so...
If there's one thing eternal, that's what's eternal: habit.
It's the one exception to the law of impermanence.
I will never stop grasping.
So then we say, okay, the two truths.
Let's see now, what stage am I in?
Am I in the mountains-are-mountains stage?
Or the mountains-are-not-mountains stage?
Am I approaching the mountains or mountains?
But which one of the mountains?
So we worry about such things: which is the truth that I'm seeing?
I was thinking about this and I said, what is truth anyway?
Did you ever think about this?
Who made up that idea of truth?
I have no idea who made that up.
I'm sure it was Aristotle.
He made everything up.
Somebody like that must have made up the idea of truth.
It's an outrageous idea, the truth.
Do we need such an idea?
Why did they think of it in the first place?
I always think of Heidegger, who resurrected a Greek word for truth, aletheia, which literally means to uncover.
That was the Greek word for truth, and at its root it means to uncover or disclose, or dis-cover.
So aletheia, the a part.
Or aletheia.
I'm not sure how you say it.
The a part is like the un in uncover or the dis in disclose, and the letheia part is the part that means to be hidden or covered.
I'm not sure, but I think it might be related to the name of the potion that you drink when you cross the river into the underworld, which causes you to forget everything that happened before.
I think Plato or somebody believed in this, that you already know everything, and when you're born you forget it all.
Something like that.
So when you learn something, actually you're not learning anything.
You're just remembering something you already knew but had forgotten.
So there's all this behind the idea of truth in the Greek tradition, which is our philosophical underpinning of the way we look at things.
Even though we have no idea what anybody in the Greek said, we all automatically have those ideas, right, because it's just carried along in the culture.

So truth is that things are hidden, they're undisclosed to us, and we're trying to bring them forth, disclose them, bring them out from their hiddenness, or let things come forth toward us to disclose themselves so that we can meet them in their disclosure.
I think that's a wonderful thought.
It seems true to me that the world is inherently hidden, and we ourselves are inherently hidden to ourselves, like they say, hidden in plain sight.
To disclose, to open up what is closed, what is hidden, means not that we can force that, but that we have to let things be things.
We have to let ourselves be ourselves.
And this is the thing: we're such meddlers.
We're not letting anything be itself.
We're always trying to meddle with things, and this causes them to hide, this causes them to resist our advances.
We also will remain essentially hidden to ourselves the more we try to meddle with ourselves.
We will miss our own heartbreaking beauty, and that's the trouble with all ideas about truth and all grasping.
We grab something and we notice there's nothing in our hand, which makes us want to grab all the more in our desperation.
If we can stop grabbing, we will be amazed.
So here's another story, the eleventh story of the Wumenguan, with Master Zhaozhou as the protagonist.
*Zhaozhou came upon a hermit and asked, "Have you got it?
Have you got it?"
The hermit held up his fist and Zhaozhou said, "This water is too shallow.
You can't anchor a boat here."
And he left.
Then he comes to another hermit, and he says, "Have you got it?
Have you got it?"
The hermit held up his fist.
Zhaozhou says, "Ah, wow, able to take, able to give, able to kill, able to give life," and he bows deeply.*
So that's the story of Zhaozhou and the hermits.
Then Wumen comments on this story.
Well, as we would say, wait a minute.
They both held up their fists in exactly the same way.
So how come one is right and the other one is wrong?
What's going on here?
And then Wumen, in his usual challenging way, says:
*If you can give a single turning word to clarify this, you will see that Zhaozhou's tongue has no bone in it.
Now helping others, now knocking them down with great freedom.
Be that as it may, Zhaozhou was himself thoroughly examined by the two hermits.
If you say there is a difference in attainment between the two hermits, you don't have the eye of practice.
If you say there is no difference of attainment, you also don't have the eye of practice.*
So that's Wumen's helpful comment.
You may think that this story is a kind of joke, and you would be right.
I think it is a kind of joke.
Because we human beings are all too easy to poke fun at.
We are all of us so foolish, so earnest, so serious, so entangled up in ourselves.
It really is rather comical.
So this is a story in which the joke is on us.
Probably most of us, when we hear this, are baffled, because we're thinking there's something going on here in Zen practice.
We know there's some truth, some reality that we can see that's somehow being pointed to in all these Zen stories and all the meditation and everything.
There's something here to be gotten.
And so we're all earnestly trying to get it.
We're working real hard.
What is it, though, that we're trying to get?
What does it mean when the hermit holds up a fist?
How come one fist is right and one fist is wrong?
Aren't we all like this?
Don't we all prefer being right to wrong?
Don't you feel good when you're right and not so great when you're wrong?
Would you rather get it or not get it?
We would rather get it, right?
We don't want to be the poor sap that doesn't get it.
But get what?
What is right and wrong anyway?
I can tell you what right and wrong is.
It's suffering.
That's what it is.
So then we say, okay, good, got that.
There's no right and wrong.
And that's right.
But if there's no right and wrong, how could that be right?
It can't be right or wrong.
Now what?
We're not used to this at all.
This is really disturbing.
But it's pretty clear.
Zhaozhou is saying one of these hermits is right and the other one is wrong.

And Wuman is saying, when he says Zhaozhou's tongue has no bone in it and Zhaozhou is raising one and disparaging the other with great freedom, that Zhaozhou's saying this one's right and this one's wrong.
It's pretty arbitrary.
He doesn't have any standard on which he's basing this.
There's no basis for him saying one is right and one is wrong.
That's the joke.
That's the joke.
But the thing is that this is happening all the time in our lives.
The world will do that.
The world will decide this one is right and this one is wrong, and we will be subject to those judgments.
It's like when you come to sesshin and somebody corrects you about the way you're standing or bowing or where you put your cushion.
And it seems like, oh, jeez, there's a right way to do it, and I've been doing it the wrong way.
Yeah.
Right.
You were doing it the wrong way and they told you how to do it the right way.
But actually, they just made it up.
Collectively, we made this up, right?
When you really get familiar with the Zen forms, you realize there's an infinitely different way of doing them.
Sometimes you bow this way, sometimes that way, depending on the circumstances, the configuration of the room.

It's always funny to me when people are trying to get it just right, and they don't realize that the reason you bow in this particular way is because in the 14th century the dharma hall was facing south or something like that.
But our dharma hall doesn't face south.
Why?
Because it used to be a school room.
It wasn't built as a dharma hall.
So, in other words, there's an infinite variety to these things, and it just depends.
When someone corrects us, we don't have to think, oh no, I was wrong.
We can just relax.
There's nothing to get mad about, nothing to get upset about, or feel guilty about, or stupid about.
And this is one reason why the Zen forms are such great teachers.
They show you, again and again, how much you are stuck on right and wrong.
If you get them wrong, it's uncomfortable, but it's just as crazy to think you have them right.

But when you have them wrong, especially when you first come to sesshin and you do everything wrong, you look at all the other people and they look to you, every one of them, like the grand inquisitor.
You know that everyone is looking at you, and you know that they all think you're doing it wrong.
You're projecting onto them your inner grand inquisitor that you've been carrying around with you for years.
So, in the story, Zhaozhou is quizzing these hermits about their Zen attainment.
Have you got it?
Have you got it?
Have you got it?
If there's nothing to get, why would he ask this question?
So yeah, there is something to get.
But what?
Well, one gets it, and the other one doesn't.
And yet there really is nothing to get.
We were talking about this the other day.
If the one who gets it is happy and proud because he gets it, then he doesn't get it.
Right?
If the one who doesn't get it is chagrined and embarrassed and resentful because he doesn't get it, then he doesn't get it either.
If the one who gets it knows there's nothing to get, and therefore he doesn't get it, then he gets it.

If the one who doesn't get it knows there's nothing to get, so the other one who's getting it is wonderful, it's just as good as him, and he's glad that together at least one of us gets it, then he gets it.
Right?
But I realize this is getting slightly ridiculous.
So if there's nothing to get, what in the world are we talking about for 50 years or so, or however long we've been talking about this?
And what are we so worried about?
One may well think, after hearing this talk, let's forget the whole thing.
Why bother with all of this complicated Zen rigamarole?
And that's a good question.
And I don't think there's any answer.
But it does remind me of some of my favorite lines from Dogen.
I'm always quoting from a poem of Dogen's:
*Effort without desire, clear water all the way to the bottom, a fish swims like a fish, vast sky transparent throughout, a bird flies like a bird.*
It also reminds me of the story that Dogen tells at the end of his chapter, Genjokoan.
Mayu was fanning himself.
And a monk came and said, "Master, the nature of the wind is permanent, and it reaches everywhere.
So why are you fanning yourself?"
And Mayu said, "Although you understand that the nature of the wind is permanent, you don't understand the meaning of its reaching everywhere."
So the monk said, "Well, what is the meaning of its reaching everywhere?"
And Mayu just kept fanning himself.
The monk bowed deeply.
So this is Dogen's way of answering the question.
If there really is nothing to get, if everything no matter what we do is empty and perfect and connected in love and compassion, why do we need to bother to practice?
Don't we do things generally for some good reason?
Don't we have a point to our activity?
Don't we try to speak the truth, not just sing a bunch of notes?
But if we understand, really understand these things, of course we will practice.
And we will know there is no way not to practice.
Practice is a word that we give to describe the activity of living beings in a living world.
Truth is everywhere all of the time.
We don't need a word for it.

Just like we were saying the other day that the Jewish mystics taught us, our job is to repair the world, to awaken broken shards, to allow the divine effulgence to express itself in each and everything.
And that's why we fan ourselves.
This doesn't cause the wind to reach everywhere.
The wind already reaches everywhere.
But this is the way a person lives when she knows that the wind reaches everywhere.
So we come back to Ching Yuen's question from the opening story.
Is there a difference between these three levels?
Rivers are rivers, rivers are not rivers, rivers are rivers?
No.
There is no difference.
We don't gain a deeper perspective, a different perspective.
There is no perspective.
Life is always life.
It appears as it appears.
We need it as we need it in this moment.
When Zhaozhou asks the hermits, have you got it? he is not asking them, have you got something?
Have you got the Zen thing?
He is asking them, do you know that there is no Zen thing?
And that's the Zen thing.
And both of the hermits, of course, get it.
Even if Zhaozhou, to make a good story, pantomimes one getting it and the other not, I don't think Zhaozhou thinks one got it and the other one doesn't.
They are all just having fun.
They are all just having fun.
This is why Wuman says it looks like he is testing them but they are really testing him.
And this is always the way it is.
This story is going on all the time.
Did you get it?
Did you get it?
Yes?
No?
Right?
Wrong?
Everything is always testing us.
All the time.
Every moment.
So yes, you've got to love our practice.
It is pretty funny.
People often say, oh, I like you, you have a good sense of humor.
But it is not me.
It is Zen.
Our tradition deeply confronts the Buddha's deepest truth and comes to the realization that actually it is very funny.
When you really see what the Buddha is telling, it is really funny.
Life is really funny.
We live, we die, we go on and on and on making the same stupid mistakes, singing the same songs.
It is so odd and funny and tragic and sad and beautiful.

And because we know this so well, we come, some of us even from far away, to spend a week wasting our time, sitting here in silence together, while some guy occasionally shows up to do stand-up, or in this case, sit-down comedy, to entertain us as we go on and on suffering and being ecstatic and wondering whether or not time is passing.
I know that some of you, as we can tell by our outfits, remember that song?
*I see by your outfit that you are a cowboy.
I see by your outfit that you are a cowboy.
If you get an outfit, you'll be a cowboy too.*
So anybody can get an outfit and you can be a Zen cowboy.
You just need an outfit.
It takes some trouble to get the outfit, I admit, but you can get it.
Anyway, you can tell by our outfits that some of us are used to these Zen routines and others are not.
And conventional truth tells us that all these routines and these rituals are this added extra thing, not really necessary, bothersome, old-fashioned, but we can tolerate it if we have to.
We don't really need it though.

And if we were really smart, we would get rid of it all and strip this down to the essential scientific meditation practice that will plasticize our brains and make us happier and more compassionate people.
Forget the rest of this other stuff.
And this is a point of view that I do appreciate and I have always supported.
No, I really do.
I think it's wonderful.
But I think also it misses something, probably.
What it misses is the joke.

Because when we go to all this trouble to create sacred space together, carefully, seriously, by the way we walk, the way we stand, the way we sit, the way we bow, the way we chant, the way we work, the way we eat the meal, it means that we can really enter a different life.
We can feel our lives differently in that space.
When I put on my robe, I just become Buddha's disciple.
I'm eating Buddha's food, I'm wearing Buddha's clothes, I'm singing Buddha's songs.
And it's wonderful for me to disappear into my robe, disappear into the cushion, disappear into the zendo, into the sky.
And I'm free from the burden of being myself.
Free from the burden of have I got it or have I not got it.
And then I take off my robe and I'm just another guy on the airplane, somebody else.
And I merge with whatever my new situation is.
It's just the way it is, no more and no less.
It's not conventional, it's not ultimate, it's just the way it is.
I get to swim like a fish sometimes when the water is deep, and I get to fly like a bird sometimes with the aid of the pilot and everybody else.
But either way, I know my element is unlimited and clear.
So I will finish today with another story.
This one is the story of Rebbe Nachman, one of my favorite stories.
Maybe you've heard this one before.
Rebbe Nachman was a genius religious person, one of the greatest religious persons of all times.
And he was especially good at telling stories.
He's famous for telling stories.
He told some stories that were so complicated that to this day nobody understands anything about them.
Some of his stories were very simple, short and wonderful.
And this is one of the simple short ones that you could easily understand.
Once upon a time, there was a king, and he said to his close minister, "I'm an astrologer, I can predict the future.
And I have studied the zodiacal signs, and I know that this year the harvest of grain is going to cause everyone who eats it to go crazy.
This is a big problem.
What's your advice?"
So the advisor said, "Well, here's my advice.
Command that a certain amount of the grain of this year, which is not making people crazy, be held aside, just enough to sustain you and me for a year.
That way we won't have to eat the crazy-making harvest, and we'll be okay, and we'll be able to guide the country.
That's my advice."
The king thought this over and he said, "Well, but if we did that, yes, we would remain sane, but then everybody else would be crazy and they would say we're crazy.
And if we held back enough grain for everybody, well, that's impossible."
So the advisor said, "Well, you make a good point there.
What do you think we should do?"
And the king said, "Here's what I think we should do.
I think we should eat the grain that everybody else is eating and go crazy along with everybody else.
However, I think we should put on each one of us a little dot, like a little blue dot on our foreheads.
And then, when we look at each other, that little dot will remind us that we're crazy.
That's what I think we should do."
That's the story.
So I think by now we all understand exactly what we have to do.
That's what I feel like when I look at all my dear Dharma friends of many years.
As soon as I look at you, I realize, yes, we are all crazy.
What a relief.
What a relief.
So this is my profound message to you today.
With a light spirit, but with a strong effort, let's all continue our sesshin until the last drop.
And let's see, do we get it or not?

verbatim.text: Well, I'm always thinking, what am I going to say to these nice people tomorrow? So I'm thinking about it, you know, during the day. And I know that many of you have been sitting with me for decades, and I'm sure that you have already heard everything that I could possibly say by now. What am I going to say now that is going to impress you after all this? And even though I generally don't repeat any talks, at least not in the same place, I'm sure that I just keep saying the same things over and over and over again.

In fact, I'm sure that I've said just that, even though I'm trying to have something new to say. I'm really racking my brains, you know, to keep you entertained, but no matter how hard I try, at some point it occurs to me, I keep saying the same things over and over and over again, or the same one thing over and over again, which I guess would happen to any of us if we kept on talking long enough. But it occurs to me that this is exactly what's happening to all of us. We are all

talking every single day, all of us, and we're all saying the same things over and over and over again. You get the magazine and it has the new article in it that everybody's emailing everybody else about, and it's this brand new idea, which when you think about it, it's the same idea from before, only wearing a different outfit. And all the new people are saying the same things that the old people used to say.

It's really amazing, and yet we remain perplexed and we keep thinking, my god, I've never heard that before. Sometimes if you find yourself in a room full of people, maybe at a restaurant, listen to the talk. Everybody's talking right in the restaurant at the same time. Just listen to the talk, and it's this sort of like

weird murmuring sound without any words in it. No meaning, no words. Kind of like traffic or ocean waves, the kind of music of human voices that rises and falls in pitch. Maybe the meaning in the end is just musical. So I've been singing and we've been singing together this week the old

human songs that we keep on singing over and over again. And Buddha was also singing songs. That's what I meant yesterday when I said that Buddha wasn't really concerned about what's right or what's true. He saw that already there was a problem with the truth. There's already a problem with the effort to get it right. So he

just wanted to figure out a way to help us so that we wouldn't have to suffer as much. So he kept trying out different songs, different keys, different notes, different rhythms and harmonies in the hope that just the sound of his voice would somehow offer us some support.
